The risk of bias in the study by Collee (1991) was downgraded by one level due to unclear or high risk of bias in several areas, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, compliance, and other potential sources of bias. 2. Inconsistency was not assessed because only one study was included in this analysis. 3. Indirectness was downgraded by one level because the analysis included only one study, and it is unclear whether the findings are representative of all high-income country settings. 4. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to wide confidence intervals that were consistent with the possibility of benefit, no effect, or harm, as well as a low number of participants. 5. The study by Imamura (2016) was downgraded by one level for risk of bias due to unclear or high risk in areas such as blinding of participants, care providers, and outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and compliance. 6. Indirectness was downgraded by one level because only one study was included in this subgroup analysis, and it is unclear whether the findings are representative of all lowand middle-income country settings. 7. Imprecision was downgraded by one level despite narrow confidence intervals around the effect estimate showing little to no difference, due to the low number of participants. 8. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to wide confidence intervals consistent with the possibility of harm, no effect, or benefit, and a low number of participants. 9. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels because there were no events in either group and the number of participants was very low. 10. The WHO guideline on the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults includes a summary of evidence-to-decision (ETD) considerations. These include confidence intervals (CI), mean differences (MD), and risk ratios (RR). 11. The follow-up time for the studies ranged between 2 and 12 weeks. 12. Risk of bias was downgraded by one level in studies due to unclear or high risk in areas such as random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants, care providers, and outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, compliance, and other biases. 13. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level due to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 51%), which was not clearly explained by subgroup analyses of high-income versus lowand middle-income country settings. 14. Imprecision was downgraded by one level due to wide confidence intervals consistent with the possibility of benefit and no effect, as well as a low number of participants. This outcome was not downgraded further for imprecision because it was already downgraded for inconsistency, which contributed to the severity of imprecision. 15. The benefits and harms of local anesthetic injections for managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and over, were compared with no intervention. The evidence was summarized for the WHO guideline on non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults. 16. Herbal medicines were defined by the WHO as herbs, herbal materials, herbal preparations, and finished herbal products containing active ingredients derived from parts of plants or plant materials. For this guideline, herbal medicines were restricted to plants or parts of plants used for medicinal purposes, administered orally or applied topically. This definition excludes plant substances smoked, individual chemicals derived from plants, or synthetic chemicals based on plant constituents. 17. Some participants adopted alternative treatments, such as traditional or herbal medicines, as part of their self-management approach when conventional treatments failed. Some viewed this as experimental to find a solution. However, many participants did not inform their healthcare providers about using these treatments. 18. The ETD process for certain herbal medicines, such as Devil's claw (Harpagophytum procumbens), white willow (Salix spp.), Brazilian arnica (Solidago chilensis), ginger (Zingiber officinale), white lily (Lilium candidum), and combination herbal compresses or transdermal patches, was not completed due to the limited number of trials contributing to the evidence base. 19. The benefits and harms of cayenne pepper (Capsicum frutescens) in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and over, were compared to placebo or no intervention. However, no trials were identified for this comparison. 20. Risk of bias was downgraded by one level in studies due to unclear or high risk of selection bias, attrition bias, reporting bias, baseline group similarity, and compliance. 21. Imprecision was downgraded by one level due to the low number of events. 22. Inconsistency was not assessed because no meta-analysis was performed. 23. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to the inability to pool data reported as relative median change from baseline and the small sample size. 24. Substantial heterogeneity (I² = 73%) was observed, and inconsistency was downgraded by one level as it was not explained by subgroup analyses. 25. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to wide confidence intervals encompassing potential benefit, no effect, and potential harm. 26. Indirectness was downgraded by one level because baseline consumption of medication was not reported. Tramadol was provided as rescue medication by trial investigators, but instructions to participants were unclear.
